title: Satisficing thresholds: econ evaluation notes for lower-cost configs (WIP)
body:
Purpose:
This note captures thinking and a proposed operational approach for applying 'satisficing thresholds' (i.e., minimum acceptable quality gates) when serving lower-cost model/server configurations. The aim is to make cheaper configs eligible for production traffic while bounding regression risk and cost-of-quality exposure.

Scope / problem statement:
- Teams want to route a portion of traffic to cheaper variants (quantized weights, smaller models, lower-precision kernels, or slower batching that reduces infra footprint).
- Naive rollouts risk silent quality regressions that only surface in production, or cost overhead from over-testing.
- We need a repeatable eval + gating framework that ties to the cost model spreadsheet inputs so product and infra can reason about unit economics versus allowed quality delta.

Core idea (satisficing thresholds):
- Define minimum acceptable performance on a prioritized eval suite (primary metrics and secondary checks). Cheaper config is eligible only if it meets the threshold.
- Thresholds are designed to be workload-aware (different for classification vs. long-form generation) and to reflect business impact, not just raw metric deltas.

Threshold types (examples):
1) Absolute threshold: metric must be >= X (e.g., chatbot answer accuracy >= 90%).
2) Relative delta: cheaper config metric >= baseline metric - delta (e.g., BLEU/EM within 2 percentage points of full model).
3) Percentile pass-rate: >= P% prompts must be within tolerance (useful when distributions are heavy-tailed).
4) Failure-mode checks: no specific failure class (e.g., hallucination rate) exceeds Y%.

Connecting to the cost model spreadsheet (what inputs matter):
- Per-token infra cost for each config (GPU hour cost converted to per-token using throughput curves).
- Expected token consumption distribution across request types (from product telemetry).
- Eval compute cost (how much it costs to run the eval harness for each variant per run).
- Expected rollout traffic fraction and duration (used to compute expected spend if quality gate passes).
- Opportunity cost of rollback (time to detect + user impact).
- Net expected savings = (per-token cost_delta * expected_tokens * traffic_fraction * duration) - (eval-run-cost + monitoring/obs overhead).

Calibration process (proposed):
1) Select representative eval suite slices: core flows (30–50%), edge cases (20%), adversarial regressions (10%), random holdout (40%) — overlapping buckets allowed.
2) Run baseline (production pinned variant) and candidate cheaper configs on the suite. Collect metrics: mean, std, percentiles, fail types.
3) Compute cost delta using current cost model spreadsheet snapshot (tag the sheet version).
4) For each candidate, compute expected savings at multiple traffic fractions and compute NPV-like expected savings for a 30/90/180 day window.
5) Propose thresholds: start conservative (relative delta <= 1.5% for critical metrics) then expand if monitoring shows low risk.

Example threshold table (illustrative):
- Short-answer retrieval accuracy (production baseline 92%): cheaper config must be >= 90% OR within relative delta 2.
- Long-form helpfulness (human eval mean 4.3/5): cheaper config must have mean >= 4.1 and no more than 5% of responses flagged catastrophic.
- Latency-sensitive routes: absolute 99th percentile latency must remain below SL; if not, disqualify regardless of quality.

Eval budget and sampling guidance:
- Per candidate run: aim for 5k–20k prompts depending on metric variance. Low-variance metrics (embedding cosine stability) can use smaller samples. Adversarial/regression tests should be kept larger.
- Use stratified sampling to preserve distribution of prompt lengths, user cohorts, and product routes.
- Maintain a reproducible seed and keep eval harness code and data pinned.

Rollout playbook (stages):
- Local dev/test: engineering validates correctness, basic checks.
- CI eval: run unit-level evals automatically on PRs to catch obvious regressions (fast, cheap).
- Canary: route 1%–5% traffic for 24–72h; gated by satisficing thresholds on production-like evals and automated user-sentinel metrics (error rate, NPS proxies).
- Incremental ramp: 5% -> 25% -> 50% following success windows, with automated guardrails (if any metric breaches, immediate rollback to baseline).
- Full rollout: only after prolonged stability and real-cost savings observed matching spreadsheet projections.

Instrumentation and monitoring to enforce gates:
- Per-variant evaluation pipeline that runs nightly (or on new model build) and pushes metric deltas to a gating service.
- Alerting thresholds tied to both absolute and relative metrics (e.g., delta_accuracy > 1.5% triggers severity P1 if route is critical).
- Drift detection: track prompt distribution shifts and re-evaluate candidate configs when distribution moves beyond a KL threshold.
- Post-rollout canaries: inline sampling of human-rated prompts (small fraction) for signal-rich checks.

Automation recommendations (Console + infra):
- Expose gate decisions as a named policy in Console: policy includes evaluation artifact id, thresholds, rollback actions, and target routes.
- Allow automatic fallback on per-request basis: if variant fails soft checks, fallback to baseline with tracing metadata for analysis.
- Capture the cost_model_version used for any decision in the rollout audit log.

Failure modes and mitigations:
- False pass due to overfitting eval sets: rotate eval data and use a holdout that is refreshed monthly.
- Silent distribution drift post-rollout: implement drift alerts and retrigger full eval when triggered.
- Hidden catastrophic failures on rare prompts: include targeted adversarial sets that exercise hallucination and safety boundaries.
- Underestimated infra scaling costs: validate throughput curves under expected batch and sequence length distributions in infra staging.

Suggested conservative numeric defaults (starting point):
- Critical accuracy metrics: relative delta <= 1.5 percentage points OR absolute >= baseline - 1.5pp.
- Helpfulness/human metrics: mean delta <= 0.2 on 5-point scale, catastrophic rate <= 5% of baseline.
- Latency: 95th/99th must be within SLO budget for route; if not, disqualify.
- Minimum eval sample per candidate: 10k prompts unless metric variance allows fewer.

Open questions / trade-offs to resolve:
- How to weight cost savings vs. potential brand impact for small but visible regressions? (product/marketing risk tolerances vary.)
- Should we permit config-specific nonuniform thresholds (e.g., allow slightly worse fluency for an embedding-focused route)?
- How to charge eval-run costs back to product teams to avoid over-testing?

Operational next steps (concrete):
- Owner: Priya Nair. Collaborators: Ethan Park (runtime), Marina Lopez (eval infra).
- Short-term (2–4 weeks): prototype one satisficing policy for the "assistant-short-answer" route, run against three candidate quantized variants, produce cost-savings / risk table. (Jira: ENGINF-4821).
- Medium-term (6–12 weeks): implement gating policy model in Console, add audit trail linking to cost model version. Begin one controlled rollout.
- Long-term: bake this into the Optimize product (expose suggested thresholds and cost tradeoffs to customers).

Appendix: minimal fields to persist with each eval run (for auditability):
- eval_run_id, date, baseline_model_sha, candidate_model_sha, cost_model_version, sample_size, metrics_snapshot (as CSV or time series id), artifacts (PR links), notes.

Notes / sign-offs required:
- Product and Legal should sign off on allowed catastrophic failure rates for customer-visible routes.
- Security to confirm adversarial tests cover relevant safety/PII leak modes.

Quick links / references:
- Cost model spreadsheet (canonical): docs.get/redwood/cost-models/optimize-v3 (link in Confluence).
- Existing related docs: confluence:OPT-SAT-12, product/optimize playbooks.
- PR placeholder: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1298 (eval harness changes).

Status: draft — seeking feedback on numeric defaults, sampling plan, and Console automation scope.
